text:
I. A messenger came to Shatili:
– The Kists have done us harm,
they have raided our shepherds,
they are wicked, of evil character.

Aluda Ketelauri is a man of grace,
He sits at the head of the council, his words are wise;
He cut off the right hands of many Kists, testing his sharp blade.
Why would a worthless man need enemies? A good man always has them!

The Kists have driven off the horses, Aluda’s winged one too.
They intend to cross the mountainous head of Arkhoti,
To shake with their horseshoes the dewy grass of the mountains.

It is the hour of dawn, the swift falcon of the cliff pursues the foe. At daybreak, the snowcock rang a bell in the crags; the dogs are sleeping on the high pasture, the sheep have not yet spread out.

– Are you not hit, you infidel dog?! – Mutsali said to him.
– Do not think I am hit, you infidel dog, a servant of the Cross of Gudani.
The sound of Aluda’s rifle was like the thunder of the heavens.
– Didn't it hit you, you dog-faith? – he calls out to him again.
– Nothing is wrong with Mutsal, you dog-faith, he was showering me with rock splinters…
– Oho, his hat is pierced, he trims the tips of his hair.
– You missed high, poor wretch, the skull bone is unharmed. Mutsal’s rifle fired, the bullet makes a harsh sound, shattering Ketelauri’s horn powder flask.
– Don't you feel it even now, you infidel dog? – he taunts him with this as well.

– Nothing is wrong, no, infidel dog, with the servant of the Gudani Cross,
The Cross follows him to victory, entreating the power of God.
It did not hit the heart, do not think it so, it was shattering the powder pouch.
Since it comes to slaughter, I will not swallow the enemy's spite.

The Shatilian’s shot shatters the Kist’s breastbone.
“Do you not feel it even now, you infidel dog?!” he screams at the Kist.
– It is in my heart, in my heart, you dog-faith! Woe to Mutsal’s aim! You have killed my brother, kill me too; what shall I say to the grace of God?

Mutsal does not desire death,
He does not lose the wolf’s hue,
He tears and stuffs into his wound the green grass of the mountain.
He fired once more at Aluda,
Wasting no time in the attempt.
He threw the rifle to Aluda,
And says one more word:
– Now let it be yours, dog-of-a-faith,
Lest it fall into the hands of another.

The word died on his lips, he sprawled down on the ground. Aluda does not want the rifle, he wept like a woman; he does not strip the weapons, his eye is not greedy. At the head he placed the dagger, inlaid with ivory, on the chest he placed the armor-piece, on the arm the Frankish sword. He does not cut the right hand of Mutsali, he said: “It is a sin; O brave man, killed by me, may God grant rest to your soul. Let your right hand remain on your arm, it is rightfully yours, let your hand turn to dust upon your heart, let the fortress gate not rejoice, you had a good nurturer, may God grant long life to your kin!” Lengthwise he covered him with a felt cloak, and placed the shield over it.

The ibexes clung to the glacier, God’s grace upon their horns.
From gorge to gorge croaks a raven of evil voice:
“Mutsali the Kist has died, I must eat the eyes of the youth,
Tear out his heart and liver, and shroud his shoulder with my wing.”

Shatili has not yet been reached by the light of the midday sun,
They will not let the traveler in, a sky of rock covers it.
A youth came over the hills, he is not pleased with himself;
Mists have settled on his face, flowing from the heart, black.
On the wall-bench hangs the arm of Mutsa’s brother,
A silver-adorned Bazala, that Khorosnuli sword.
It was bound to the crags, where Imeda’s fortress stands,
In summer it listens for the gun’s report, in winter the avalanche descends.
Many times the downpour caught him, the black raven croaked.
The insatiable vulture hovered over his head,
No one could snatch his luck, no one could do him ill.
Like the hands of an infidel, the scorching sun rays melt upon it.
The snake could not pierce the foundation, it is still alive today.
Sometimes the storm comes, sometimes the sun shines, it is fair.
What of it, it has seen many dead with bristling mustaches!
Many times the torrent of the slain’s blood has flowed to the meadows;
The evil water of Ardoti has been dyed red.

Whoever thirsts for enmity, let him open the door of his house,
Let him pool blood in the hearth, standing in it himself.
Let him drink it as wine, let it be used as bread.
Let him cross himself, as if he were in a church.
Let him have his wedding in blood, let the cross be signed there,
Let him invite guests, let him line up the host.
Let him make his bed in blood, let his spouse lie by his side,
Let him have many children, many sons and daughters;
Let him dig a grave right there, let the dead be buried there.
If you kill another, you too will be killed; the clan will not let the killer go unpunished.

At Shatil, Khevsur women and daughters-in-law stepped out onto the roofs,
Three of Aluda’s brothers and nephews came out to meet him.
Many want to hear the news, many others have come.
They congratulate Aluda: – May you be a man of renown!
Old Ushisha asks Aluda for news of the encounter.
Ketelauri tells the story of the Ghilghvelian wolf:
“Leaving from here, Ushisha, I cut across the mountain trail,
I caught up by a shortcut. I spotted his tracks in the sand.
There were two of them, I used my rifle, I could not reach with the tip of my sword.
That late Mutsal, he had iron for a heart!”

– “What are you saying? The salvation of a Kist was never written in our creed.”
– “That is why I praise his valor; it cannot be bought with money.
Three times I fired, three times he did; with the third, I finished it.
The bullet striking his chest shredded his heart.
He stuffed the wound with moss, and so he breathed his last.
Even as his soul struggled to depart, he spoke once more of his faith.”

We say, "We are the men, only our mothers raise us; we shall be saved, while the infidels await their gasping in the pitch." By saying this we talk idly; the children of God know better. Do all speak the truth, whoever may swear an oath?!

I could not bring myself to cut off Mutsal’s right hand,
My heart grew angry, it would not do what is hard to do:
“Let my fame be diminished, I am better for you as a counselor.”

They turned their backs on Aluda with faces full of wrath;
They headed to their own houses with attics and doors.
They forsook Ketelauri with hearts full of thorns,
Calling out Aluda’s name with mournful cries.

To Shatili Mindia also came with a bronze-colored horse,
With a Frankish sword girded at his waist, with a shielded arm,
The slayer of twelve Kists with a long-shafted spear.
Reddish Mindia resembled a deer with a moon-like forehead.

They spoke ill of Aluda with poisonous words.
He took offense, his brow furrowed with a fearsome frown.
– "Do not speak ill of a brave man with a flighty tongue.
May your enemy perish easily, let me hear the truth plainly.
No need for much sorrow, one day's provisions will suffice me,
I shall not lose my way, I know the path in every direction.
Mindia shall come to you this very day, before many others arrive."
He struck with his heel, the chestnut sped, moving like a whirlwind.

III. It has grown dark, the waters weep, the mantle of night covers us; it is the time of the stars' shimmering, of dew settling upon the grass, of dead souls emerging from the grave, the time of their quiet song.

The giants emerge from the rocks, wandering through the ravines.
Everyone has supped and now they prepare for sleep.
“Eat some bread,” Aluda’s sister and mother implore him.
“I want no bread, mother, my heart is heavy for some reason,
Last night I saw ill dreams, I was in a gathering somewhere.
A dead man lay before us, the Khevsurs sat in sorrow.
Prepared for a raid, some stood at the doors.
I too was there, weeping, as is the custom of a man.
I had a premonition of the raid, and the time to depart had come.”

In an instant, someone seized my hand and placed the hilt of a dagger within it. I looked; it was Mutsali, clad in chainmail of bronze. Upon his chest, the mark of me and that moment of battle was visible; the gray fibers of brdzami were spread within his bullet wound. He stood like a rock, unyielding, with no tear falling from his eye.

„I want death, yet I do not die; kill me,“ he told me imploringly. „May this fleeting world remain to you, while I depart from the earth; have your fill, children of the Khevsurs, of raiding and the brandishing of swords.“

I sat down; someone set a bowl before me; it was a stew of human flesh.
I ate, though the bony human hands and feet filled me with horror.
"What am I doing?" I lamented, monstrous and accursed.
"Eat," Rama called to me, "do not be dazed: serve me more of Aluda's heated meat and broth." They served me more meat and broth, seasoned with a man's mustache...
Dreams have tormented me; that is why I am troubled in spirit.

IV. Day breaks, the mountain peaks turned red, mists gathered upon the mountains.
The village rises, awakens, travelers pass to and fro on the roads.
The vultures set out on their journey, casting their eyes over mountain and vale;
In so much fluttering they are, yet they could leave no trace upon the sky!

"Who comes on a red horse, having crossed the water?"
"– Welcome in peace!"
– The Khevsurs called out to Mindia.
"– What news have you brought?"
– They shouted to him from afar.

– Youths, your blood boils, you cut and sew with your heart,
You let the heart drag the mind, you let your head be severed by the axe,
You cannot easily recognize a brave man by his manly law!
Do not let one oppress the other, heart and mind are brothers.
Aluda is right, even if the heavens should collapse upon me!
If you do not believe, here is the Kist’s severed arm.
Keep your tongue in its scabbard, do not utter words lightly,
Do not easily say of a brave man that he is of no use!
They handed the hand to Aluda: – Take it, fix it to the gate!

– If I had wanted to cut off the hand, could I not have cut it myself?
I cannot do right by you, Mindia, I will settle the matter ill;
Why do I need it? It cannot wield a sword, it is of no use as a shield;
If I take it to the mountains, it will not mow, nor serve as a hay-hook.
Take it away, if you believe in God, let my eyes see it no more.
It is the right hand of a brave youth, my heart burns with pity.
Why are the Khevsurians angry, why do they burst with rage?!
I will kill an enemy, but I will not cut off his right hand to satisfy their spite!
“It is not the custom to kill an enemy, if you do not cut off his hand with a knife.”
Woe to such justice, christened with sin and guilt!

V. The Lord’s time has come. The people flocked to the shrine festival: they must inform the Master, whoever was suffering from any pain. Men and women gathered with offerings, with sheep and with oxen; they presented the offerings to the Master at the granary door.
Who is this who has approached, like a mist, with a brass-bound Naziki sword? He gives a bullock to the Elder of the Gorge, standing with a bowed head.

– Whom do you favor, Aluda, with this black bullock? –
The priest asks Aluda with his sleeve rolled back.
Great is our Lord, the Cross of Gudani at the head,
He has strong subjects too, by God and by God's power.
The Lord loves a good man, he does not grudge him grace;
Brave men of hope are destined for our Lord.
Tell me the name, for whom you sacrifice, may it be accepted for them. –
He draws his dagger, preparing to speak the words of glory.

– That is an offering, Berdia, for the Kist slain just now.
Mutsal was his name, the son of the unbaptized.
Bless it well for me; I have dedicated it for him,
As for a handsome brother killed against my will.

– You would hallow the faithless? That will not befit you,
To slaughter a sacrifice for a Kist will not serve you well.
No such custom comes from father, nor grandfather, nor great-grandfather,
Come to your senses, you are a Christian, you turn infidel by this;
Do not follow the devil… how did such a word escape your lips?!
How many others have you slain? On your wall, hands hang like withered boughs,
Some of Lek, others of Kist—a bridge of right hands;
You never slaughtered even a kid for any, let alone a great bull.
How can I offer to the Lord a dog, one of the breed of dogs?
Rather let the heavens collapse upon me, let the earth’s back split beneath me,
Or let the bottomless sea swallow me, that I might dine on sand!
Berdia’s face changes color, a color of a different kind of fear.
– Do not belittle my gift, if God's grace favors you, I too am a servant of the Gudani Cross, a Khevsur of your own waters, as if we are one, Berdia, dwellers of the same mountain.
– You strive in vain, Aluda, in vain you waste your breath.

Ketelauri grew enraged, he took on the color of a wolf;
He reached for his Frankish sword, a light like the sun flashed out.
He struck the bull upon the neck, the head rolls on the ground.
At the same time he pleaded with the Lord: "Do not spare me, your child,
Let this be an offering for Mutsal, for that unbaptized hero."

Berdia Jagarashvili turns his face toward the people.
“Has it ever been heard,” he cried, “such a forsaking of the faith:
Aluda slaughters the sacrifice himself, commemorating the soul of a Kist,
People, I want to hear the answer of your hearts.
Assemble, sons of Khevsureti, all of you – great and small,
Let us do justice, let us break the beams of Aluda’s house;
Do not show mercy, be the ones who make his wife and children weep.
Let him be banished, a gazer at the sky and clouds of another land.
Go, break the doors of his dark house and tower.
Set fire to the haystacks – let the flames reach the sky,
Drive out the sheep, cows, and oxen for the community.
Make his wife and children weep in Shatili, and the kinswomen and women in Gudani;
May our Lord be wrathful, he is not to be pitied.

Hearing this, Mindia’s eyes filled with tears,
He can no longer help Aluda, he crosses his arms over his chest,
The armed sons of Khevsureti readied their shields,
They must strike Ketelauri, the bronze rings out fiercely.
Over the Khevsurs gathered in a circle, a boy appeared,
In one hand he held the gnawed bones of a right hand.

– Take it away, – says Berdia, – the limb of an infidel dog,
We, the sons of Khevsureti, are not servants of the devil, of the Ali.
They threw the hand of Mutsal’s arm to a dog to eat.
The cur did not touch it; it broke into a howl of pity.

Khevisberi Berdia says:
– Khevsurs, see with your own eyes:
"A dog does not break a dog's bone,"
It has been said from the very beginning.
Children drag the Kist's right hand
Down below with a hook.

VI. It snows, the wind rages, the necks of the mountains are bound;
Avalanches descend into the ravine, sloughed from the cliffs.
The ice has bound in blue the banks and reaches of the waters,
The narrow paths of the roads are completely drifted over.
Who has grown weary of life, who will set out on the path? Ahead goes the traveler, carving the way, and five follow behind. Distressed by hunger, a pack of wolves howls at the mountain.
"May you see no good, Khevsurians," a woman cries out in anger. "Alas, our home, stone no longer stands upon stone; upon the tower, upon the pillars of the loft, now the ravens are perching."

Mother would say to Aluda: – My son, walk slowly, neither I nor your wife Lela can endure without you, the children have grown restless, our limbs are frozen with hardship. Alas, how pathless we wander, alas, how dark it is! Will the Khevsurians not need your help?! What waters or meadows will host us, where will we waste away? Homeless and hearthless, we shall perish elsewhere too. We can no longer reach our home, across the Shatili valley. To forsake one’s own land and water is exceedingly hard; I have taken the hue of the dying, my mind has grown dizzy. My knees fail me, darkness has stood like a pillar in my heart. Alas, graves of our forefathers, rocks, standing sharp!

Aluda says with sorrow:
– Women, do not be prattling,
Come, follow me, let us depart,
God has granted this as our fate,
Do not offend the Cross, do not curse the community,
Do not turn foolish!

Once Aluda desired, once to turn his head:
"Farewell, ibex-haunts, gladdeners of the eye!
Farewell, my home and hearth, stirrer of sorrow in the heart!
Farewell, our Lord, giver of strength to your servants!"

The travelers forever forsook their own land and water. The mountain peaks stand stunned; the howling of the wind is heard. They passed, they crossed the ridge, the trace of their trail is no longer seen. Only from afar was heard the bitter sobbing of a woman.
